$comment: True / False / Not Given mức Passage 2, LinguaFlow tự soạn (2–3 đoạn văn, câu hỏi paraphrase, bẫy từ tuyệt đối / so sánh / mốc thời gian / 'believed' vs 'proved'). Đoạn văn cách nhau bằng dòng trống. a: T | F | NG. ev: câu trong bài làm căn cứ (để tô sáng), không có với NG. w: giải thích, chỉ ra cặp từ đồng nghĩa và vì sao FALSE (bài nói NGƯỢC lại) hay NOT GIVEN (bài KHÔNG nói tới).

passages.title: The box that changed trade
passages.text:
Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow and labour-intensive. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels and crates of every size, and teams of dockworkers carried them on board one by one. A vessel could spend almost as long in port as it did at sea, and theft of cargo was common.

The American trucking businessman Malcolm McLean is widely credited with popularising the steel shipping container. In 1956 his converted tanker, the Ideal X, carried 58 containers from Newark to Houston. McLean later claimed that the cost of loading fell from several dollars per ton to just a few cents, although historians note that his figures were never independently checked. Within two decades, ports that refused to invest in cranes and storage yards for containers began to lose business to those that did, and many traditional dock jobs disappeared.

q.s: In the period before containers, ships often remained in port for a long time.
q.ev: A vessel could spend almost as long in port as it did at sea
q.w: 'remained in port for a long time' ≈ 'spend almost as long in port as it did at sea' → TRUE.

q.s: McLean was the first person to invent the steel shipping container.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói McLean được ghi nhận là người PHỔ BIẾN (popularising) container, không nói ông có PHÁT MINH ra nó hay không, cũng không nói ai phát minh. 'popularise' ≠ 'invent' → NOT GIVEN, không phải FALSE vì bài không phủ nhận.

q.s: The Ideal X had originally been built for a different purpose.
q.ev: his converted tanker, the Ideal X
q.w: 'converted tanker' = tàu chở dầu được hoán cải → ban đầu đóng cho mục đích khác → TRUE. Từ khoá dễ bỏ qua: converted.

q.s: McLean's claims about lower loading costs have been confirmed by historians.
q.ev: historians note that his figures were never independently checked
q.w: Bài nói số liệu của ông CHƯA BAO GIỜ được kiểm chứng độc lập → ngược với 'confirmed' → FALSE.

q.s: Ports that did not adapt to containers lost some of their trade.
q.ev: ports that refused to invest in cranes and storage yards for containers began to lose business to those that did
q.w: 'did not adapt' ≈ 'refused to invest'; 'lost some of their trade' ≈ 'lose business' → TRUE.

passages.title: Learning from the dance of bees
passages.text:
For centuries beekeepers noticed that a single bee returning to the hive could somehow lead others to a new source of food, but the mechanism remained a mystery. In the 1940s the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch proposed that bees communicate through a 'waggle dance', in which the angle of the dance relative to the vertical indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun, while the length of the waggling phase signals distance.

Von Frisch's interpretation was not accepted immediately. Some researchers argued that bees found food mainly by smell, and the debate continued for several decades. The question was largely settled in the 2000s, when scientists used radar to track individual bees after they had watched a dance and found that they flew towards the location the dance had indicated. Von Frisch himself had shared a Nobel Prize in 1973, long before this confirmation arrived.

q.s: Beekeepers were unaware that bees could guide each other to food until the twentieth century.
q.ev: For centuries beekeepers noticed that a single bee returning to the hive could somehow lead others to a new source of food
q.w: Bài nói người nuôi ong đã NHẬN THẤY điều này hàng thế kỷ; chỉ CƠ CHẾ là bí ẩn. Câu hỏi nói họ không hề biết → ngược lại → FALSE.

q.s: According to von Frisch, the duration of part of the dance shows how far away the food is.
q.ev: the length of the waggling phase signals distance
q.w: 'duration of part of the dance' ≈ 'length of the waggling phase'; 'how far away' ≈ 'distance' → TRUE.

q.s: Researchers who believed in the role of smell carried out more experiments than von Frisch.
q.w: Bài có nhắc nhóm cho rằng ong tìm mồi bằng mùi, nhưng KHÔNG so sánh số thí nghiệm. Bẫy so sánh 'more … than' → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Radar studies supported von Frisch's explanation.
q.ev: found that they flew towards the location the dance had indicated
q.w: Ong bay đúng hướng điệu nhảy chỉ → ủng hộ giả thuyết. 'supported' ≈ 'largely settled' → TRUE.

q.s: Von Frisch received the Nobel Prize after his theory had been confirmed by radar.
q.ev: Von Frisch himself had shared a Nobel Prize in 1973, long before this confirmation arrived.
q.w: Nobel năm 1973, TRƯỚC khi radar xác nhận (những năm 2000) → thứ tự ngược → FALSE.

passages.title: Where coffee really began
passages.text:
A popular legend tells of an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi who noticed his goats becoming unusually energetic after eating the red berries of a certain shrub. The story is charming, but it does not appear in writing until the late seventeenth century, more than a thousand years after the events it supposedly describes, and most historians treat it as folklore.

The earliest reliable evidence of coffee drinking comes from fifteenth-century Yemen, where members of Sufi religious communities used the drink to stay awake during night-time prayers. From there coffee spread to Mecca and Cairo, and by the sixteenth century coffee houses had become lively centres of conversation in Istanbul. Not everyone welcomed them: on several occasions religious and political authorities tried to close coffee houses, fearing that they encouraged criticism of those in power. These bans were rarely effective for long.

q.s: The story of Kaldi was first recorded shortly after the events took place.
q.ev: it does not appear in writing until the late seventeenth century, more than a thousand years after the events it supposedly describes
q.w: Ghi chép đầu tiên cách sự kiện HƠN 1000 năm → ngược với 'shortly after' → FALSE.

q.s: Most historians doubt that the Kaldi story is true.
q.ev: most historians treat it as folklore
q.w: 'treat it as folklore' (coi là truyện dân gian) ≈ 'doubt that it is true' → TRUE.

q.s: Coffee was first grown as a crop in Yemen.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói bằng chứng UỐNG cà phê sớm nhất ở Yemen; không nói nơi đầu tiên TRỒNG cà phê. 'drinking' ≠ 'grown as a crop' → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Sufi communities drank coffee to help them remain alert at night.
q.ev: used the drink to stay awake during night-time prayers
q.w: 'remain alert' ≈ 'stay awake'; 'at night' ≈ 'night-time' → TRUE.

q.s: Attempts to ban coffee houses usually succeeded in the long term.
q.ev: These bans were rarely effective for long.
q.w: 'rarely effective for long' = hiếm khi hiệu quả lâu dài → ngược với 'usually succeeded in the long term' → FALSE.

passages.title: Cities that trap heat
passages.text:
On a summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This 'urban heat island' effect occurs because materials such as asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while the shortage of trees and open water reduces natural cooling. Waste heat from vehicles and air-conditioning units adds to the problem.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. During heatwaves, death rates in the hottest urban districts tend to rise faster than in cooler ones, with elderly residents especially at risk. Some cities have responded by painting roofs white, planting street trees and creating small parks. Researchers caution, however, that the benefits of such measures vary considerably from one city to another, depending on local climate and building density, and that no single solution suits every location.

q.s: City centres are warmer than rural areas only during the daytime.
q.ev: On a summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside.
q.w: Bài nói rõ BUỔI TỐI trung tâm vẫn nóng hơn, và vật liệu toả nhiệt sau hoàng hôn → 'only during the daytime' bị phủ nhận → FALSE. Bẫy từ tuyệt đối 'only'.

q.s: A lack of vegetation contributes to higher urban temperatures.
q.ev: the shortage of trees and open water reduces natural cooling
q.w: 'lack of vegetation' ≈ 'shortage of trees' → TRUE.

q.s: Air-conditioning is the main cause of the urban heat island effect.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói nhiệt thải từ điều hoà 'adds to the problem' (góp thêm), không xếp hạng nguyên nhân chính. Bài cũng không phủ nhận → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Older people face particular danger in hot city districts during heatwaves.
q.ev: with elderly residents especially at risk
q.w: 'older people' ≈ 'elderly residents'; 'particular danger' ≈ 'especially at risk' → TRUE.

q.s: Experts agree that white roofs are the most effective measure for all cities.
q.ev: no single solution suits every location
q.w: Chuyên gia nói lợi ích khác nhau tuỳ thành phố và không giải pháp nào hợp mọi nơi → ngược với 'most effective for all cities' → FALSE.

passages.title: Before Gutenberg
passages.text:
Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, developed in Mainz around 1450, is often described as the invention that made the modern world possible. It is less widely known that movable type had been used in East Asia centuries earlier. Records describe a Chinese craftsman, Bi Sheng, who made individual characters from baked clay in the eleventh century, and in Korea the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type dates from 1377.

Why, then, did printing transform Europe so rapidly? One explanation lies in the writing systems involved. Chinese requires thousands of distinct characters, so preparing and sorting type was enormously time-consuming, and many Asian printers continued to prefer carved wooden blocks. European alphabets, by contrast, need fewer than a hundred symbols including capitals and punctuation. Gutenberg also adapted the screw press used by winemakers and developed an oil-based ink that stuck to metal type, although it is unclear how many of these ideas were entirely his own.

q.s: Movable type was in use in Asia before Gutenberg built his press.
q.ev: movable type had been used in East Asia centuries earlier
q.w: 'before Gutenberg' ≈ 'centuries earlier' → TRUE.

q.s: Bi Sheng's type was made of metal.
q.ev: made individual characters from baked clay
q.w: Bi Sheng dùng ĐẤT SÉT nung; kim loại là của Hàn Quốc năm 1377. Bẫy gán nhầm chi tiết → FALSE.

q.s: The 1377 Korean book was the first book ever printed with metal type.
q.w: Bài nói đây là cuốn sách in kim loại CÒN SÓT LẠI cổ nhất ('oldest surviving'), không nói là cuốn ĐẦU TIÊN từng được in. 'oldest surviving' ≠ 'first ever' → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Some printers in Asia preferred to keep using wooden blocks.
q.ev: many Asian printers continued to prefer carved wooden blocks
q.w: 'keep using' ≈ 'continued to prefer' → TRUE.

q.s: Historians are certain that Gutenberg invented oil-based ink without help from others.
q.ev: it is unclear how many of these ideas were entirely his own
q.w: Bài nói KHÔNG RÕ bao nhiêu ý tưởng là của riêng ông → ngược với 'certain' → FALSE.

passages.title: Sleep and memory
passages.text:
Scientists have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory, but only in recent decades have experiments begun to show how. In a typical study, volunteers learn a list of word pairs or a simple motor task in the evening. Half are then allowed a normal night's sleep, while the other half are kept awake. When both groups are tested again after a period of recovery sleep, those who slept immediately after learning usually perform better.

Recordings of brain activity suggest that during deep sleep, the hippocampus 'replays' patterns of activity from the day, which may help transfer new information into long-term storage. However, researchers stress that most of these experiments have involved young, healthy adults in laboratory settings. Whether the same effects apply equally to older people, or to the complex skills learned at school and work, is still being investigated.

q.s: The link between sleep and memory was first proposed only a few decades ago.
q.ev: Scientists have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory
q.w: Giả thuyết đã có từ LÂU ('long suspected'); chỉ bằng chứng thực nghiệm mới gần đây → FALSE.

q.s: In the experiments described, all participants were eventually allowed to sleep before the final test.
q.ev: When both groups are tested again after a period of recovery sleep
q.w: Cả hai nhóm đều được ngủ bù ('recovery sleep') trước khi kiểm tra lại → TRUE. Đây là câu khó vì phải hiểu chi tiết quy trình.

q.s: Word pairs are easier to remember than motor tasks after sleep.
q.w: Bài nêu cả hai loại bài tập nhưng không so sánh loại nào dễ nhớ hơn → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: The hippocampus may be involved in moving new memories into long-term storage.
q.ev: which may help transfer new information into long-term storage
q.w: 'moving' ≈ 'transfer'; câu hỏi giữ 'may' giống bài → TRUE.

q.s: It has been proven that the effect is equally strong in older adults.
q.ev: Whether the same effects apply equally to older people, or to the complex skills learned at school and work, is still being investigated.
q.w: Bài nói vẫn ĐANG nghiên cứu → chưa chứng minh. 'proven' mâu thuẫn với 'still being investigated' → FALSE.

passages.title: Turning seawater into drinking water
passages.text:
Desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, has been practised on a small scale for centuries; sailors once boiled seawater and collected the steam. Large modern plants mostly use a process called reverse osmosis, in which seawater is pushed at high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass but block salt. The method requires far less energy than the older thermal plants that dominated the industry until the 1990s.

Even so, desalinated water remains more expensive than water taken from rivers or underground sources in most places. A further concern is brine, the highly salty waste left over from the process. If it is released carelessly, it can harm marine life near the outlet pipes. Countries in the Middle East currently operate a large share of the world's desalination capacity, and several are investing in solar power to run new plants.

q.s: Desalination is a technology that was invented in the twentieth century.
q.ev: has been practised on a small scale for centuries
q.w: Bài nói đã được thực hiện quy mô nhỏ hàng THẾ KỶ (thuỷ thủ đun nước biển) → FALSE.

q.s: Reverse osmosis consumes less energy than thermal desalination.
q.ev: The method requires far less energy than the older thermal plants
q.w: 'consumes less energy' ≈ 'requires far less energy' → TRUE.

q.s: In most locations, desalinated water now costs less than river water.
q.ev: desalinated water remains more expensive than water taken from rivers or underground sources in most places
q.w: Bài: vẫn ĐẮT HƠN ở hầu hết nơi → ngược lại → FALSE.

q.s: Most desalination plants treat brine before releasing it into the sea.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói nếu xả brine bừa bãi thì có thể hại sinh vật biển; không nói các nhà máy có xử lý brine hay không, cũng không nói 'hầu hết' → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Some Middle Eastern countries plan to use solar energy for desalination.
q.ev: several are investing in solar power to run new plants
q.w: 'plan to use solar energy' ≈ 'investing in solar power to run new plants' → TRUE.

passages.title: The road that was never called silk
passages.text:
The network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East and the Mediterranean is today known as the Silk Road. Yet the people who used these routes never called them by this name. The term was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, and it became widely popular only in the twentieth century.

The name is also misleading in other ways. There was no single road but a shifting web of paths across deserts and mountains, and few merchants travelled the whole distance; goods usually passed through many hands, with each trader covering one section. Silk was certainly an important export from China, but the routes also carried spices, glass, metals, horses and paper. Perhaps most significantly, they spread ideas and religions: Buddhism, for example, travelled from India into China along these paths.

q.s: Traders in ancient times referred to these routes as the Silk Road.
q.ev: the people who used these routes never called them by this name
q.w: Người dùng các tuyến này KHÔNG BAO GIỜ gọi chúng bằng tên đó → FALSE.

q.s: Von Richthofen's term was immediately adopted by most scholars.
q.ev: it became widely popular only in the twentieth century
q.w: Năm 1877 đặt tên nhưng chỉ phổ biến ở thế kỷ 20 → không phải 'immediately' → FALSE.

q.s: Most goods were carried along the routes by a series of different merchants.
q.ev: goods usually passed through many hands, with each trader covering one section
q.w: 'a series of different merchants' ≈ 'passed through many hands'; 'most' ≈ 'usually' → TRUE.

q.s: Silk was the most valuable product traded along the routes.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói lụa là mặt hàng 'important', không nói có GIÁ TRỊ NHẤT hay không → NOT GIVEN. Bẫy so sánh nhất.

q.s: Religious beliefs were among the things that spread along the routes.
q.ev: they spread ideas and religions
q.w: 'religious beliefs' ≈ 'religions' → TRUE.

passages.title: Forests at the edge of the sea
passages.text:
Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow in the salty, muddy water of tropical coastlines. Their dense, tangled roots slow down waves and trap sediment, which helps to protect coastal communities from storms and erosion. Studies after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami suggested that villages behind healthy mangrove belts sometimes suffered less damage, although scientists disagree about how much protection forests can offer against very large waves.

Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon in their waterlogged soils, where dead plant material decays slowly. Despite these benefits, a significant proportion of the world's mangroves were cleared in the late twentieth century, largely to make room for shrimp farms and coastal development. Replanting projects have since been launched in many countries, but their success rate has been mixed: seedlings planted in the wrong position on the shore often fail to survive.

q.s: Mangrove roots help to reduce the force of waves.
q.ev: Their dense, tangled roots slow down waves
q.w: 'reduce the force of waves' ≈ 'slow down waves' → TRUE.

q.s: Scientists agree that mangroves can fully protect villages from large tsunamis.
q.ev: scientists disagree about how much protection forests can offer against very large waves
q.w: Các nhà khoa học BẤT ĐỒNG → ngược với 'agree … fully protect' → FALSE.

q.s: Plant material breaks down quickly in mangrove soils.
q.ev: where dead plant material decays slowly
q.w: 'breaks down quickly' ngược với 'decays slowly' → FALSE.

q.s: Shrimp farming was one of the main reasons for the loss of mangroves.
q.ev: largely to make room for shrimp farms and coastal development
q.w: 'main reasons' ≈ 'largely to make room for' → TRUE.

q.s: Most replanting projects have been organised by international charities.
q.w: Bài không nói ai tổ chức các dự án trồng lại → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Two languages, one brain
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, many educators believed that bringing up a child with two languages would cause confusion and slow down learning. Research from the 1960s onwards challenged this view, and by the 2000s a number of studies were reporting that bilingual people performed better on tasks requiring them to switch attention or ignore distractions. This so-called 'bilingual advantage' attracted enormous media coverage.

More recently, however, the picture has become less clear. Several large studies have failed to reproduce the advantage, and some researchers argue that earlier positive results were more likely to be published than negative ones. Others reply that bilingualism takes many forms and that the effects may depend on how often, and in what situations, people use each language. What almost all researchers now accept is that learning two languages does not harm a child's overall development.

q.s: In the past, some teachers thought that learning two languages was bad for children.
q.ev: many educators believed that bringing up a child with two languages would cause confusion and slow down learning
q.w: 'bad for children' ≈ 'cause confusion and slow down learning'; 'some teachers' ≈ 'many educators' → TRUE.

q.s: The bilingual advantage was first identified in the 1960s.
q.ev: by the 2000s a number of studies were reporting that bilingual people performed better
q.w: Những năm 1960 chỉ là lúc nghiên cứu bắt đầu phản bác quan điểm cũ; 'bilingual advantage' được báo cáo vào những năm 2000 → FALSE. Bẫy gán sai mốc thời gian.

q.s: Recent large studies have consistently confirmed the bilingual advantage.
q.ev: Several large studies have failed to reproduce the advantage
q.w: Nhiều nghiên cứu lớn KHÔNG lặp lại được kết quả → ngược với 'consistently confirmed' → FALSE.

q.s: Bilingual children usually achieve higher marks at school.
q.w: Bài nói về bài tập chuyển sự chú ý, không nhắc điểm số ở trường → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Most researchers agree that bilingualism is not harmful to children's development.
q.ev: learning two languages does not harm a child's overall development
q.w: 'most researchers agree' ≈ 'almost all researchers now accept' → TRUE.

passages.title: Keeping vaccines cold
passages.text:
Many vaccines lose their effectiveness if they become too warm, and some are damaged by freezing. Moving them from factory to patient therefore depends on a 'cold chain': an unbroken series of refrigerated stores, vehicles and containers that keep the product within a narrow temperature range, usually between 2°C and 8°C. A single failure at any point can make a whole shipment useless, often without any visible sign.

The final stage of the journey is frequently the most difficult. In remote rural areas, health workers may need to carry vaccines for hours on foot or by motorbike to villages without a reliable electricity supply. Insulated boxes packed with ice, solar-powered refrigerators and small temperature indicators that change colour when a vaccine has been exposed to heat have all helped. Nevertheless, the World Health Organization has estimated that a considerable share of vaccines is wasted globally each year, and temperature problems are one of the causes.

q.s: All vaccines can be safely frozen during transport.
q.ev: some are damaged by freezing
q.w: Một số vaccine bị HỎNG khi đông lạnh → 'all … safely frozen' bị phủ nhận → FALSE.

q.s: It is usually easy to see when a vaccine has been spoiled by temperature changes.
q.ev: often without any visible sign
q.w: Thường KHÔNG có dấu hiệu nhìn thấy được → ngược với 'easy to see' → FALSE.

q.s: The last part of the delivery process often presents the greatest challenges.
q.ev: The final stage of the journey is frequently the most difficult.
q.w: 'last part' ≈ 'final stage'; 'greatest challenges' ≈ 'most difficult' → TRUE.

q.s: Solar-powered refrigerators are more reliable than ice boxes.
q.w: Bài liệt kê cả hai giải pháp đều có ích nhưng không so sánh độ tin cậy → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Temperature problems are the only reason vaccines are wasted.
q.ev: temperature problems are one of the causes
q.w: Nhiệt độ chỉ là MỘT TRONG các nguyên nhân → ngược với 'only reason' → FALSE.

passages.title: From beads to windows
passages.text:
Archaeologists believe that the first true glass objects were beads made in Mesopotamia around 4,500 years ago. For many centuries afterwards, glass remained a luxury. Craftsmen shaped it by winding hot glass around a core of clay or by pressing it into moulds, methods that were slow and produced only small items such as jewellery and perfume bottles.

The situation changed dramatically in the first century BC, when craftsmen on the eastern Mediterranean coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated by blowing through a hollow tube. Glassblowing allowed vessels to be made quickly and cheaply, and under the Roman Empire glass cups and bottles became common household objects. The Romans also produced the first glass windows, although these were thick, uneven and far from transparent. Clear window glass of good quality did not become widely available in Europe until many centuries later.

q.s: The earliest glass objects were probably made in Mesopotamia.
q.ev: Archaeologists believe that the first true glass objects were beads made in Mesopotamia
q.w: 'probably' ≈ 'archaeologists believe' (mức độ chắc chắn tương đương) → TRUE.

q.s: Before glassblowing, glass could be used to make only small objects.
q.ev: methods that were slow and produced only small items such as jewellery and perfume bottles
q.w: 'only small objects' ≈ 'only small items' → TRUE.

q.s: Glassblowing was invented by the Romans.
q.ev: craftsmen on the eastern Mediterranean coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated
q.w: Thổi thuỷ tinh do thợ ở bờ ĐÔNG Địa Trung Hải phát hiện; người La Mã chỉ phổ biến đồ thuỷ tinh. Bẫy gán sai chủ thể → FALSE.

q.s: Glass objects were expensive for ordinary Roman families.
q.ev: under the Roman Empire glass cups and bottles became common household objects
q.w: Cốc, chai thuỷ tinh trở thành đồ gia dụng PHỔ BIẾN và làm 'cheaply' → ngược với 'expensive' → FALSE.

q.s: Roman glass windows were mainly used in public buildings.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói cửa kính La Mã dày, không đều, không trong; không nói dùng ở loại công trình nào → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: The invention of paper
passages.text:
According to traditional Chinese accounts, paper was invented in AD 105 by Cai Lun, an official at the imperial court, who made sheets from tree bark, old rags and fishing nets. Archaeological discoveries, however, have shown that a simple form of paper existed in China at least two centuries before this date. Cai Lun's contribution may therefore have been to improve the process and present it to the emperor, rather than to create it from nothing.

For several hundred years the technique remained largely within China. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century, and paper mills were soon operating in Baghdad. Europeans were slower to adopt the material, partly because parchment made from animal skin was already well established for important documents. By the time printing presses appeared in Europe, however, paper had become essential, since it was far cheaper to produce in large quantities.

q.s: Cai Lun used recycled materials to make paper.
q.ev: made sheets from tree bark, old rags and fishing nets
q.w: 'old rags and fishing nets' = vải vụn, lưới cũ → vật liệu tái sử dụng → TRUE.

q.s: Archaeological evidence supports the traditional date for the invention of paper.
q.ev: a simple form of paper existed in China at least two centuries before this date
q.w: Khảo cổ cho thấy giấy đã có ít nhất 200 năm TRƯỚC năm 105 → mâu thuẫn với mốc truyền thống → FALSE.

q.s: Cai Lun was punished for claiming to have invented paper.
q.w: Bài không nhắc gì về việc Cai Lun bị phạt → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Paper production in Baghdad began before the technique reached China.
q.ev: For several hundred years the technique remained largely within China. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century
q.w: Giấy có ở Trung Quốc trước, rồi mới tới thế giới Hồi giáo → thứ tự ngược → FALSE.

q.s: One reason Europeans adopted paper slowly was that they already had another writing material.
q.ev: partly because parchment made from animal skin was already well established for important documents
q.w: 'another writing material' ≈ 'parchment'; 'one reason' ≈ 'partly because' → TRUE.

passages.title: Parcels from the sky
passages.text:
Delivery by drone has been promoted for over a decade as a fast and environmentally friendly alternative to vans. Small drones can avoid traffic altogether, and for light parcels travelling short distances they may produce lower emissions per package than road vehicles. Trials in several countries have focused on medical supplies, such as blood samples and medicines, where speed is especially valuable.

Large-scale commercial services, however, have grown more slowly than early supporters predicted. Most drones can carry only a few kilograms, and their range is limited by battery capacity. Regulators in many countries require operators to keep drones within the pilot's line of sight unless special permission is granted, which makes long-distance deliveries difficult. Public attitudes also matter: surveys indicate that some residents are concerned about noise and privacy. Industry analysts expect drones to complement, rather than replace, conventional delivery vehicles.

q.s: Drones are less polluting than vans in every type of delivery.
q.ev: for light parcels travelling short distances they may produce lower emissions per package than road vehicles
q.w: Bài giới hạn: chỉ với hàng NHẸ, quãng NGẮN và chỉ 'may' → không phải 'every type' → FALSE.

q.s: Medical deliveries have been a focus of drone trials.
q.ev: Trials in several countries have focused on medical supplies
q.w: Paraphrase gần như trực tiếp → TRUE.

q.s: Commercial drone delivery has expanded faster than was originally expected.
q.ev: Large-scale commercial services, however, have grown more slowly than early supporters predicted.
q.w: Tăng CHẬM HƠN dự đoán → ngược lại → FALSE.

q.s: Special permission can allow drones to fly beyond the pilot's view.
q.ev: keep drones within the pilot's line of sight unless special permission is granted
q.w: 'unless special permission is granted' → có giấy phép đặc biệt thì được bay ngoài tầm nhìn → TRUE. Đọc kỹ 'unless'.

q.s: Most residents in trial areas support drone deliveries.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói MỘT SỐ cư dân lo ngại tiếng ồn, quyền riêng tư; không nói tỉ lệ ủng hộ → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: The clever octopus
passages.text:
Octopuses have around 500 million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but unusually, about two-thirds of these are located in their arms rather than in the central brain. This arrangement appears to allow each arm a degree of independence; an arm that has been separated from the body can still respond to touch and grasp objects for a short time.

In laboratory experiments, octopuses have learned to open screw-top jars, find their way through mazes and distinguish between different shapes. Some aquarium staff have reported individuals escaping from their tanks at night and returning before morning, although such stories are difficult to verify. What makes octopus intelligence particularly interesting to biologists is that it evolved quite separately from that of mammals and birds. Since octopuses live for only one or two years and receive no care from their parents, they must learn quickly on their own.

q.s: Most of an octopus's neurons are found outside its central brain.
q.ev: about two-thirds of these are located in their arms rather than in the central brain
q.w: Hai phần ba ở tay = phần lớn nằm ngoài não trung tâm → TRUE.

q.s: An octopus arm stops functioning immediately once it is cut off.
q.ev: an arm that has been separated from the body can still respond to touch and grasp objects for a short time
q.w: Tay bị tách VẪN phản ứng một thời gian → ngược với 'immediately' → FALSE.

q.s: Octopuses learned to solve mazes more quickly than dogs.
q.w: Bài so sánh số neuron với chó, nhưng không so sánh tốc độ giải mê cung → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Reports of octopuses leaving their tanks at night have been scientifically confirmed.
q.ev: although such stories are difficult to verify
q.w: Những câu chuyện này KHÓ kiểm chứng → không phải 'confirmed' → FALSE.

q.s: Young octopuses learn without help from their parents.
q.ev: receive no care from their parents, they must learn quickly on their own
q.w: 'without help from their parents' ≈ 'receive no care … on their own' → TRUE.

passages.title: Roofs that grow
passages.text:
A green roof is a roof partly or completely covered with plants growing in a layer of soil or another growing medium. Although the idea is often presented as modern, grass-covered roofs have been used for centuries in Scandinavia, where they provided insulation against harsh winters. Today green roofs are promoted mainly for their environmental benefits in cities.

The plants and soil absorb rainwater, which reduces the amount flowing into drains during heavy storms, and they can lower the temperature of the roof surface on hot days. Green roofs may also provide habitats for insects and birds. On the other hand, they are more expensive to install than conventional roofs, and the building must be strong enough to support the extra weight, particularly when the soil is saturated with water. In some cities, including Toronto, new buildings above a certain size are required by law to include a green roof.

q.s: Green roofs are a completely new invention.
q.ev: grass-covered roofs have been used for centuries in Scandinavia
q.w: Mái phủ cỏ đã có hàng THẾ KỶ ở Bắc Âu → FALSE.

q.s: Scandinavian grass roofs helped to keep buildings warm.
q.ev: they provided insulation against harsh winters
q.w: 'keep buildings warm' ≈ 'insulation against harsh winters' → TRUE.

q.s: Green roofs can reduce pressure on drainage systems during storms.
q.ev: reduces the amount flowing into drains during heavy storms
q.w: 'reduce pressure on drainage systems' ≈ 'reduces the amount flowing into drains' → TRUE.

q.s: Green roofs are cheaper to maintain than ordinary roofs over time.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói LẮP ĐẶT đắt hơn; không nói chi phí BẢO TRÌ về lâu dài → NOT GIVEN. Bẫy: 'install' ≠ 'maintain'.

q.s: In Toronto, every new building must have a green roof.
q.ev: new buildings above a certain size are required by law to include a green roof
q.w: Chỉ toà nhà TRÊN một kích thước nhất định → không phải 'every' → FALSE.

passages.title: Railway time
passages.text:
Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, set by the position of the sun. When it was noon in London, it was a few minutes earlier in Bristol, further west. This caused few problems when travel was slow, but the arrival of the railways made the differences confusing and even dangerous, since timetables became difficult to coordinate.

In 1840 the Great Western Railway in Britain began using London time at all its stations, and other companies soon followed. By the late 1840s most British railways had adopted this 'railway time', although some towns resisted for years and displayed two times on their public clocks. In the United States, with its much greater distances, railway companies introduced a system of time zones in 1883. Remarkably, this was done by the railways themselves; the system was not made official by federal law until 1918.

q.s: Before the railways, towns in the west of Britain were ahead of London in time.
q.ev: When it was noon in London, it was a few minutes earlier in Bristol, further west
q.w: Bristol (phía tây) SỚM HƠN tức là chậm hơn London, không phải 'ahead' → FALSE.

q.s: Differences in local time were considered a serious problem before trains were introduced.
q.ev: This caused few problems when travel was slow
q.w: Trước đường sắt, chênh lệch giờ gây RẤT ÍT vấn đề → FALSE.

q.s: All British towns accepted railway time immediately.
q.ev: some towns resisted for years and displayed two times on their public clocks
q.w: Một số thị trấn chống lại nhiều năm → không phải 'all … immediately' → FALSE.

q.s: The American time zone system was first introduced by railway companies.
q.ev: railway companies introduced a system of time zones in 1883
q.w: Paraphrase trực tiếp → TRUE.

q.s: American passengers complained that the 1883 system was confusing.
q.w: Bài không nhắc phản ứng của hành khách Mỹ → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Building with bamboo
passages.text:
Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some species can grow taller than many trees, and certain types grow by almost a metre in a single day. Because it can be harvested after only three to five years, compared with several decades for most timber trees, it is frequently described as one of the most sustainable building materials available.

Bamboo has been used for houses, bridges and scaffolding in Asia and South America for thousands of years. Its strength relative to its weight is impressive, and it bends rather than breaks in strong winds and earthquakes. However, untreated bamboo is vulnerable to insects and fungi and may last only a few years outdoors. Modern treatments can extend its life considerably. Engineers also point out that, unlike steel or concrete, natural bamboo varies greatly in size and strength, which has made it harder to create standard building codes for its use.

q.s: Bamboo belongs to the same plant family as trees.
q.ev: Bamboo is technically a grass
q.w: Tre về mặt khoa học là CỎ, không phải cây gỗ → FALSE.

q.s: All bamboo species can grow almost one metre a day.
q.ev: certain types grow by almost a metre in a single day
q.w: Chỉ 'certain types' (một số loại) → không phải 'all' → FALSE.

q.s: Bamboo can be harvested more quickly than most trees used for timber.
q.ev: harvested after only three to five years, compared with several decades for most timber trees
q.w: 3–5 năm so với vài chục năm → nhanh hơn → TRUE.

q.s: Bamboo buildings performed better than concrete ones in recent earthquakes.
q.w: Bài nói tre uốn cong thay vì gãy, nhưng không so sánh với bê tông trong các trận động đất cụ thể → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: The natural variation in bamboo has complicated the development of building standards.
q.ev: natural bamboo varies greatly in size and strength, which has made it harder to create standard building codes
q.w: 'complicated' ≈ 'made it harder'; 'building standards' ≈ 'standard building codes' → TRUE.

passages.title: The power of belief
passages.text:
A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, yet patients who receive one often report feeling better. In clinical trials, new drugs are compared with placebos to find out whether their benefits go beyond this effect. Placebo responses tend to be strongest for symptoms that people experience subjectively, such as pain, nausea and fatigue, and weakest for conditions that can be objectively measured, like the size of a tumour.

The way a treatment is presented also seems to matter. Some studies have found that patients respond more strongly to injections than to pills, and to expensive-looking capsules than to cheap ones. Surprisingly, a few small experiments have reported improvements even when patients were told openly that they were taking a placebo. Researchers caution that these 'open-label' studies have involved small numbers of participants and need to be repeated on a larger scale.

q.s: A placebo contains a small amount of the real medicine.
q.ev: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient
q.w: Giả dược KHÔNG có hoạt chất → FALSE.

q.s: Placebos have a greater effect on pain than on tumour size.
q.ev: strongest for symptoms that people experience subjectively, such as pain, nausea and fatigue, and weakest for conditions that can be objectively measured, like the size of a tumour
q.w: Đau: mạnh nhất; kích thước khối u: yếu nhất → so sánh đúng → TRUE.

q.s: Doctors frequently prescribe placebos to their patients.
q.w: Bài nói giả dược dùng trong thử nghiệm lâm sàng, không nói bác sĩ có thường kê giả dược hay không → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: The appearance of a treatment may influence how well it works.
q.ev: The way a treatment is presented also seems to matter.
q.w: 'appearance' ≈ 'the way a treatment is presented'; 'may' ≈ 'seems to' → TRUE.

q.s: Open-label placebo studies have been carried out with large groups of patients.
q.ev: these 'open-label' studies have involved small numbers of participants
q.w: Chỉ với SỐ ÍT người tham gia → ngược với 'large groups' → FALSE.

passages.title: A second life for batteries
passages.text:
As electric vehicles become more common, the question of what happens to their batteries at the end of their working life is growing more urgent. A car battery is usually considered unsuitable for driving once it can hold around 70 to 80 per cent of its original charge. At this point, however, it may still be useful for less demanding tasks, such as storing electricity from solar panels in homes or supporting the power grid.

Eventually, all batteries must be recycled. Lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals including lithium, cobalt and nickel, and recovering them reduces the need for new mining. Current recycling methods are energy-intensive, though, and recovering lithium in particular has often been uneconomical. The European Union has introduced rules requiring new batteries to contain a minimum proportion of recycled material in the coming years, a policy intended to encourage investment in recycling plants.

q.s: Electric car batteries are replaced when they can no longer hold any charge.
q.ev: A car battery is usually considered unsuitable for driving once it can hold around 70 to 80 per cent of its original charge.
q.w: Pin bị coi là không phù hợp khi CÒN 70–80% dung lượng, không phải khi hết hẳn → FALSE.

q.s: Used car batteries can be used to store energy in homes.
q.ev: storing electricity from solar panels in homes
q.w: Paraphrase trực tiếp → TRUE.

q.s: Recycling batteries can reduce the demand for mining.
q.ev: recovering them reduces the need for new mining
q.w: 'reduce the demand for mining' ≈ 'reduces the need for new mining' → TRUE.

q.s: Recovering lithium has always been profitable.
q.ev: recovering lithium in particular has often been uneconomical
q.w: Thu hồi lithium THƯỜNG không kinh tế → ngược với 'always profitable' → FALSE.

q.s: The European Union will provide funding to build recycling plants.
q.w: Bài nói EU đặt quy định về tỷ lệ vật liệu tái chế để KHUYẾN KHÍCH đầu tư, không nói EU trực tiếp cấp tiền → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: The food of the gods
passages.text:
Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to the tropical forests of Central and South America. Chemical traces found on ancient pottery suggest that people in the region were preparing drinks from cacao more than 3,000 years ago. These early drinks were very different from modern chocolate: they were usually bitter, often flavoured with chilli, and served frothy rather than sweet.

Among the Aztecs, cacao beans were so highly valued that they were used as a form of money, and the drink was associated mainly with rulers, warriors and wealthy merchants. When Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, it was at first an expensive drink for the aristocracy, and Europeans began adding sugar to suit their own tastes. Solid chocolate bars of the kind familiar today were not developed until the nineteenth century, when new machinery made it possible to process cacao on an industrial scale.

q.s: Cacao trees originally grew in the Americas.
q.ev: native to the tropical forests of Central and South America
q.w: 'originally grew' ≈ 'native to' → TRUE.

q.s: Early cacao drinks were sweetened with honey.
q.ev: they were usually bitter, often flavoured with chilli, and served frothy rather than sweet
q.w: Đồ uống ban đầu ĐẮNG, không ngọt → FALSE. (Nhiều bạn chọn NG vì không thấy chữ 'honey', nhưng bài đã nói rõ 'rather than sweet'.)

q.s: Among the Aztecs, cacao was drunk by all social classes equally.
q.ev: the drink was associated mainly with rulers, warriors and wealthy merchants
q.w: Chủ yếu tầng lớp trên → không phải 'all social classes equally' → FALSE.

q.s: Spanish explorers were the first Europeans to taste chocolate.
q.w: Bài nói người Tây Ban Nha mang cacao về châu Âu, nhưng không nói họ là người châu Âu ĐẦU TIÊN nếm → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Industrial machinery made modern chocolate bars possible.
q.ev: when new machinery made it possible to process cacao on an industrial scale
q.w: Thanh sô-cô-la ra đời thế kỷ 19 nhờ máy móc → TRUE.

passages.title: Stripes that changed shopping
passages.text:
The barcode is now so familiar that it is easy to forget it was once a novel idea. In 1952 two American engineers, Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, received a patent for a code made up of concentric circles, inspired partly by Morse code. Their invention was ahead of its time: the lasers and computers needed to read such codes cheaply did not yet exist, and the patent was eventually sold.

It took another two decades before the grocery industry agreed on a common standard, the Universal Product Code, which used straight lines rather than circles. In 1974, a packet of chewing gum became the first product to be scanned at a supermarket checkout in Ohio. Shop owners were initially hesitant because of the cost of scanners, but barcodes soon proved their value by speeding up checkouts and allowing stores to track stock far more accurately.

q.s: Woodland and Silver's original design used straight lines.
q.ev: a code made up of concentric circles
q.w: Thiết kế ban đầu là các vòng tròn đồng tâm; đường thẳng là của chuẩn UPC sau này → FALSE.

q.s: The technology to read barcodes cheaply was not available in 1952.
q.ev: the lasers and computers needed to read such codes cheaply did not yet exist
q.w: Paraphrase trực tiếp → TRUE.

q.s: Woodland and Silver made a large profit from selling their patent.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói bằng sáng chế cuối cùng bị bán, không nói họ có lời nhiều hay ít → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Chewing gum was the first item ever scanned in a shop.
q.ev: a packet of chewing gum became the first product to be scanned at a supermarket checkout
q.w: 'first item ever scanned in a shop' ≈ 'first product to be scanned at a supermarket checkout' → TRUE.

q.s: Shop owners welcomed barcode scanners enthusiastically from the start.
q.ev: Shop owners were initially hesitant because of the cost of scanners
q.w: Ban đầu DO DỰ → ngược với 'enthusiastically from the start' → FALSE.

passages.title: The longest journey
passages.text:
The Arctic tern is a small seabird weighing just over 100 grams, yet it makes the longest known migration of any animal. Each year it travels from its breeding grounds in the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again, enjoying two summers and more daylight than any other creature. Early estimates put the round trip at around 40,000 kilometres.

When researchers fitted terns with tiny tracking devices in the late 2000s, they discovered that the true distance was much greater. Rather than flying in a straight line, the birds followed winding routes that took advantage of prevailing winds, covering on average around 70,000 kilometres a year. Over a lifetime that can exceed thirty years, a single tern may fly a distance equivalent to three return trips to the Moon. The tracking also revealed that the birds made long stopovers in the middle of the Atlantic, where food is plentiful.

q.s: The Arctic tern is the largest bird that migrates between the Arctic and Antarctic.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói nhạn biển nhỏ (khoảng 100g); không so sánh kích thước với loài chim di cư khác. Không có câu phủ nhận → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Arctic terns experience summer twice a year.
q.ev: enjoying two summers
q.w: Đi từ Bắc Cực đến Nam Cực → hai mùa hè mỗi năm → TRUE.

q.s: Tracking studies showed that earlier distance estimates were too high.
q.ev: they discovered that the true distance was much greater
q.w: Khoảng cách thực LỚN HƠN nhiều → ước tính cũ quá THẤP, không phải quá cao → FALSE.

q.s: The terns fly directly between their summer locations.
q.ev: Rather than flying in a straight line, the birds followed winding routes
q.w: Bay đường vòng, không thẳng → FALSE.

q.s: The birds stop to feed in the Atlantic during their journey.
q.ev: the birds made long stopovers in the middle of the Atlantic, where food is plentiful
q.w: 'stop to feed' ≈ 'long stopovers … where food is plentiful' → TRUE.

passages.title: Birds in a noisy world
passages.text:
Many birds use song to defend territory and attract mates, so a song that cannot be heard is of little use. In cities, low-frequency noise from traffic and construction can mask bird calls. Studies in Europe and North America have found that some urban birds, such as great tits, sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter forests, which may help their songs to be heard above the background noise.

Other species appear to adjust the timing of their songs instead. European robins in some noisy areas have been recorded singing at night, when traffic is lighter. It is not yet clear whether these changes are learned behaviour or a result of evolution over many generations. Researchers also warn that adapting has a cost: higher-pitched songs may be less attractive to females, and birds that sing at night may lose valuable sleep.

q.s: Traffic noise can make it harder for birds to hear each other.
q.ev: low-frequency noise from traffic and construction can mask bird calls
q.w: 'mask bird calls' = che lấp tiếng chim → khó nghe nhau → TRUE.

q.s: City great tits sing at a lower pitch than forest great tits.
q.ev: sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter forests
q.w: Chim thành phố hót CAO hơn, không thấp hơn → FALSE.

q.s: All birds in noisy areas change the pitch of their song.
q.ev: Other species appear to adjust the timing of their songs instead.
q.w: Một số loài đổi THỜI ĐIỂM hót thay vì đổi cao độ → không phải 'all … change the pitch' → FALSE.

q.s: Scientists have shown that robins learn to sing at night from older birds.
q.ev: It is not yet clear whether these changes are learned behaviour or a result of evolution
q.w: Chưa rõ là học được hay do tiến hoá → không thể 'have shown … learn' → FALSE.

q.s: Noise pollution has caused some bird populations in cities to decline.
q.w: Bài nói về thay đổi cách hót và cái giá phải trả, không nói số lượng chim giảm → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Islands of spice
passages.text:
For centuries nutmeg and mace, two spices produced by the same tree, grew naturally only on the tiny Banda Islands in what is now eastern Indonesia. Arab and Asian traders carried them westwards, and by the time they reached the markets of Europe, their price had multiplied many times over. In medieval Europe, nutmeg was valued not only as a flavouring but also, wrongly, as a cure for various diseases.

In the early seventeenth century the Dutch East India Company fought to establish complete control over the islands, using extreme violence against the local population. The company tried to maintain its monopoly by allowing nutmeg trees to grow on only a few islands and by soaking exported seeds in lime so that they could not be planted elsewhere. These efforts ultimately failed: in the eighteenth century a French official succeeded in smuggling seedlings out, and nutmeg plantations were soon established in other tropical colonies.

q.s: Nutmeg and mace come from different types of tree.
q.ev: two spices produced by the same tree
q.w: Hai loại gia vị từ CÙNG một cây → FALSE.

q.s: Nutmeg was much more expensive in Europe than where it was grown.
q.ev: by the time they reached the markets of Europe, their price had multiplied many times over
q.w: 'much more expensive' ≈ 'price had multiplied many times over' → TRUE.

q.s: Nutmeg was an effective medicine in medieval Europe.
q.ev: nutmeg was valued not only as a flavouring but also, wrongly, as a cure for various diseases
q.w: Chữ 'wrongly' cho biết người ta TIN SAI rằng nó chữa bệnh → không hiệu quả → FALSE. Một chữ nhỏ quyết định đáp án.

q.s: The Dutch treated seeds so that other countries could not grow nutmeg.
q.ev: soaking exported seeds in lime so that they could not be planted elsewhere
q.w: 'treated seeds' ≈ 'soaking … in lime'; 'other countries could not grow' ≈ 'could not be planted elsewhere' → TRUE.

q.s: The French official who smuggled seedlings was later rewarded by his government.
q.w: Bài không nói viên quan Pháp có được thưởng hay không → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Plastic too small to see
passages.text:
Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres. Some are manufactured at this size, such as the tiny beads once common in facial scrubs, but most are formed when larger items break down under the effects of sunlight, waves and wear. Washing synthetic clothes also releases fibres that pass through many wastewater treatment plants.

Microplastics have now been found almost everywhere scientists have looked, from deep ocean trenches to Arctic snow, and in drinking water, seafood and human blood. Their effects on human health, however, remain uncertain. Laboratory studies have shown that very high concentrations can damage cells, but these concentrations are often far greater than those people are typically exposed to. Several countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics, though experts point out that such bans address only a small part of the problem, since microbeads make up a minor share of the total.

q.s: Most microplastics are produced deliberately at a small size.
q.ev: most are formed when larger items break down
q.w: Phần lớn hình thành do vật lớn BỊ VỠ, không phải sản xuất cố ý → FALSE.

q.s: Wastewater treatment plants remove all fibres from synthetic clothing.
q.ev: releases fibres that pass through many wastewater treatment plants
q.w: Sợi vẫn ĐI QUA nhiều nhà máy xử lý → không phải 'remove all' → FALSE.

q.s: Microplastics have been detected in the human body.
q.ev: and in drinking water, seafood and human blood
q.w: 'human body' ≈ 'human blood' → TRUE.

q.s: Scientists have proved that microplastics cause serious illness in humans.
q.ev: Their effects on human health, however, remain uncertain.
q.w: Tác động vẫn CHƯA CHẮC CHẮN → không thể 'proved' → FALSE.

q.s: Bans on microbeads have greatly reduced plastic pollution in the oceans.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói lệnh cấm giải quyết một phần nhỏ vấn đề, không nói lượng ô nhiễm đại dương đã giảm bao nhiêu → NOT GIVEN. Lưu ý: 'chỉ giải quyết phần nhỏ' khác với 'không làm giảm'.

passages.title: Working from home
passages.text:
Before 2020, working from home was relatively rare in most countries and was often regarded by managers with suspicion. The COVID-19 pandemic forced millions of office employees to work remotely almost overnight, creating what some researchers described as the largest workplace experiment in history.

The results have been mixed. Many surveys found that employees valued the time saved by not commuting and felt more productive at home. Some studies measuring actual output, however, reported smaller or even negative effects, particularly for tasks that required close teamwork or the training of new staff. A widely cited experiment at a Chinese travel company found that a hybrid arrangement, with two days a week at home, had no negative effect on performance and reduced the number of employees who resigned. As a result, many organisations have now adopted hybrid models rather than returning fully to the office.

q.s: Before the pandemic, managers generally trusted employees who worked from home.
q.ev: was often regarded by managers with suspicion
q.w: Quản lý thường NGHI NGỜ → ngược với 'generally trusted' → FALSE.

q.s: Employees often believed they worked more efficiently at home.
q.ev: felt more productive at home
q.w: 'believed they worked more efficiently' ≈ 'felt more productive' → TRUE.

q.s: All studies have shown that remote work increases output.
q.ev: Some studies measuring actual output, however, reported smaller or even negative effects
q.w: Một số nghiên cứu cho kết quả nhỏ hoặc TIÊU CỰC → không phải 'all … increases' → FALSE.

q.s: In the Chinese study, fewer staff left their jobs under the hybrid arrangement.
q.ev: reduced the number of employees who resigned
q.w: 'fewer staff left their jobs' ≈ 'reduced the number of employees who resigned' → TRUE.

q.s: Employees in the Chinese company were paid more for working from home.
q.w: Bài không nhắc đến lương → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Selling ice to the tropics
passages.text:
In the early nineteenth century, a young Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor had what most people considered a ridiculous idea: to cut ice from frozen New England ponds in winter and ship it to the hot Caribbean. His first cargo, sent to Martinique in 1806, largely melted, and Tudor lost a great deal of money. For years he struggled with debt and was even imprisoned for it.

Tudor persisted, experimenting with different insulating materials and eventually discovering that sawdust was cheap and highly effective. He also had to create demand, offering free ice to bartenders so that customers would become used to cold drinks. By the 1830s his business was shipping ice as far as India, and he became known as the 'Ice King'. The trade employed thousands of workers until the development of mechanical refrigeration in the late nineteenth century gradually made natural ice unnecessary.

q.s: Most people at the time thought Tudor's plan was likely to succeed.
q.ev: had what most people considered a ridiculous idea
q.w: Hầu hết mọi người cho là ý tưởng NỰC CƯỜI → FALSE.

q.s: Tudor's first shipment was financially unsuccessful.
q.ev: His first cargo, sent to Martinique in 1806, largely melted, and Tudor lost a great deal of money.
q.w: 'financially unsuccessful' ≈ 'lost a great deal of money' → TRUE.

q.s: Sawdust was the most expensive insulating material Tudor tried.
q.ev: sawdust was cheap and highly effective
q.w: Mùn cưa RẺ → ngược với 'most expensive' → FALSE.

q.s: Tudor gave ice away to encourage people to drink cold drinks.
q.ev: offering free ice to bartenders so that customers would become used to cold drinks
q.w: 'gave ice away' ≈ 'offering free ice' → TRUE.

q.s: Tudor's company was the first to develop mechanical refrigeration.
q.w: Bài nói làm lạnh cơ học khiến băng tự nhiên hết cần thiết, không nói ai phát triển nó → NOT GIVEN.

passages.title: Learning from mistakes in aviation
passages.text:
Commercial flying is today one of the safest forms of transport, but this was not always the case. In the 1950s and 1960s fatal accidents were far more frequent than they are now. Part of the improvement is due to better aircraft and navigation technology, but experts also credit the industry's approach to learning from errors.

When an accident occurs, independent investigators examine the wreckage and the 'black box' recorders, which store flight data and conversations in the cockpit. Their reports are usually published so that airlines around the world can apply the lessons. Many countries also run confidential systems that allow pilots to report mistakes and near-misses without fear of being punished. Some hospitals have tried to copy this approach, but progress has been slower, partly because medical staff worry that admitting mistakes could lead to legal action.

q.s: Air travel has become safer since the 1960s.
q.ev: In the 1950s and 1960s fatal accidents were far more frequent than they are now.
q.w: Tai nạn chết người khi đó nhiều hơn bây giờ → ngày nay an toàn hơn → TRUE.

q.s: Improvements in safety are due entirely to new technology.
q.ev: Part of the improvement is due to better aircraft and navigation technology, but experts also credit the industry's approach to learning from errors
q.w: Công nghệ chỉ là MỘT PHẦN; còn cách học từ lỗi → không phải 'entirely' → FALSE.

q.s: Accident investigations are carried out by the airlines themselves.
q.ev: independent investigators examine the wreckage
q.w: Điều tra viên ĐỘC LẬP, không phải chính hãng bay → FALSE.

q.s: Pilots who report their own mistakes are usually given extra training.
q.w: Bài chỉ nói phi công báo lỗi mà không sợ bị phạt; không nói có được đào tạo thêm → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Fear of legal consequences has slowed the adoption of this approach in hospitals.
q.ev: partly because medical staff worry that admitting mistakes could lead to legal action
q.w: 'fear of legal consequences' ≈ 'worry … could lead to legal action'; 'slowed' ≈ 'progress has been slower' → TRUE.

passages.title: The secret of rice terraces
passages.text:
In mountainous regions of southern China, the Philippines and Indonesia, farmers have carved steep hillsides into narrow, level fields for growing rice. Some of these terraces are believed to be more than a thousand years old. Building them required enormous collective effort, and maintaining them still depends on cooperation between families, since water must flow from one level to the next.

In Bali, the distribution of water among rice fields has traditionally been managed by community organisations known as subak, which are closely linked to local water temples. In the 1970s, government programmes encouraged farmers to plant new high-yield varieties as often as possible, ignoring the traditional schedule. Within a few years, pest outbreaks and water shortages had become serious problems. Research by the anthropologist Stephen Lansing later suggested that the temple system had been coordinating planting times in a way that limited pests, and the traditional schedule was partly restored.

q.s: All of the terraces described are over a thousand years old.
q.ev: Some of these terraces are believed to be more than a thousand years old.
q.w: Chỉ MỘT SỐ ruộng bậc thang được cho là hơn 1000 năm → không phải 'all' → FALSE.

q.s: Farmers working on terraces need to cooperate with their neighbours.
q.ev: maintaining them still depends on cooperation between families
q.w: 'cooperate with their neighbours' ≈ 'cooperation between families' → TRUE.

q.s: The subak organisations were created by the government in the 1970s.
q.ev: has traditionally been managed by community organisations known as subak
q.w: Subak là tổ chức CỘNG ĐỒNG truyền thống; chính phủ những năm 1970 lại bỏ qua lịch truyền thống → FALSE.

q.s: The new rice varieties tasted worse than traditional ones.
q.w: Bài nói giống lúa mới năng suất cao, không nói về hương vị → NOT GIVEN.

q.s: Lansing's research indicated that the traditional system helped to control pests.
q.ev: the temple system had been coordinating planting times in a way that limited pests
q.w: 'helped to control pests' ≈ 'limited pests'; 'indicated' ≈ 'suggested' → TRUE.
